title: The Salt Keeper
text:
Preface

“The sea does not drown a man because it hates him. It drowns him because it is cold, and heavy, and has nowhere else to put its weight.”
— Traditional Keeper’s Admonition

This short volume was prepared as an exercise in structural typography and digital book publishing using Quarto. All events and persons depicted herein are purely fictitious.

title: 1  The Shallows
text:
The skiff operator refused to pull alongside the iron ladder until the swell had peaked twice.
“Two weeks,” the man said, leaning over his outboard motor without killing the throttle. His voice was raw against the spray. “Not a day sooner. If the easterly holds, the spit stays submerged through the spring tides. Keep the hatch bolted after four o’clock.”
Julian Vance stepped across the wet gunwale onto the rung. The iron was encrusted with dead barnacles that bit through his woolen gloves. He did not look down at the oily black churn between the hull and the granite column. He tossed his canvas pack onto the lower gallery, climbed the nine paces, and stood on Black Rock Spit.
The beacon was not a towering white pillar of romantic postcard lore. It was a stubby, hexagonal tower of rough-faced basalt blocks, reinforced with corroded iron bands and capped by a dulled brass lantern room. It had been automated thirty years ago, then abandoned entirely when satellite navigation rendered its red sector blink redundant.
Julian watched the skiff cut a white scar across the grey chop until it shrank into the mist toward the mainland.
The silence that settled over the spit was immediate and physical. There were no gulls. The salt air did not smell of clean brine; it had the sharp, alkaline odor of lime kilns and wet slate.
Inside, the living quarters occupied the second tier—a circular chamber with a single bunk, an iron stove with a crooked flue, and a mahogany writing bureau bolted to the outer wall. A thick film of crystalline salt coated every horizontal plane: the edge of the iron kettle, the brass rim of the barometer, the woolen blanket folded on the mattress.
Julian set his rucksack down and struck a wooden match. The sulfur flared blue before taking to the tallow candle on the desk.
On the bureau lay the catalog ledger provided by the Maritime Trust. Beside it rested a leather-bound daybook, its corners swollen from humidity, with the initials T.C. pressed into the calfskin cover.
Julian rubbed his thumbs over his coat sleeves, pulled his chair out, and uncapped his pen.

title: 2  The Reading of Callow
text:
By midnight, the easterly gale had arrived, not with howling squalls, but with a rhythmic, pulsing percussion against the basalt foundations. Every wave sent a dull vibration through the flagstones, into the legs of the iron chair, and up Julian’s spine.
He opened Thomas Callow’s daybook.
The early entries from October were precise, written in the cramped, angular hand of an experienced mariner:

Oct 12. Wind WNW force 3. Visibility 6 miles. Cleaned lamp prisms of brine crust. Replaced lead gasket on freshwater cistern valve. Three fishing smacks rounded the north reef at dawn.


Oct 29. Spring tides higher than chart datum by eleven inches. Water reached third rung of gallery ladder at noon slack. Water remarkably clear. Could see bottom gravel at four fathoms. No crabs on the kelp beds.

By mid-November, the script began to widen, the pen digging deeper into the fiber of the page:

Nov 14. The cistern water has turned hard. Boiled two gallons for tea; left a residue like fine flour, but bitter on the tongue. Checked roof catchment. No sea spray reached the guttering. Where is the mineral coming from?


Nov 21. It does not dry like sea salt. When sea salt dries, it forms cubes. This dries into needles. Long, sharp needles like powdered glass. It collects along the baseboards while I sleep.

Julian paused. He raised the candle and glanced at the base of the wall behind the stove.
A faint, pale line ran the entire perimeter of the chamber. In the dim light, it looked like chalk dust. He stood, knelt beside the stonework, and scraped a fingernail along the skirting.
It came away with a cluster of microscopic, transparent filaments that sparkled under the candle flame. When he touched the tip of his finger to his tongue, there was no saline sting—only an intense, cold numbness that spread instantly across his gums.
He returned to the desk and turned the page.

Dec 02. I heard the bell buoy at South Shoal chime six times between two and three in the morning. The South Shoal buoy was dragged under and lost in the gale of ’98. There is no buoy.
Something is displacing the water from beneath.

The final entry occupied an entire page, written in jagged charcoal:

Dec 09. It is not rising up the stairs. It is condensing out of the air. Keep your mouth closed when the lantern goes out.

title: 3  The Well
text:
Julian did not sleep.
At three in the morning, the wind died completely. The sudden stillness was worse than the gale; it left only the thick, slurring suck of water sliding back and forth through the crevices beneath the floorboards.
He climbed the spiral iron staircase to the lantern room.
The lantern room was freezing. Condensation did not run down the glass panes in droplets; it clung to the glass in intricate, branching frost-patterns, despite the outdoor temperature hovering well above freezing.
Julian wiped a patch clear with his woolen cuff.
The tide was out, according to the lunar tables. The granite apron of the spit should have been exposed for eighty yards in every direction.
Instead, the water stood level with the lower gallery platform. The surface was glassy, mirror-flat, and completely devoid of foam. It did not reflect the clouds or the moon. It was an opaque, curdled grey, like melted tin.
Downstairs, the hatch latch gave a dull, metallic click.
Julian held his breath.
A soft, scraping sound followed—the friction of wet cloth sliding across rough stone. It moved slowly, pausing at the landing between the second and third tiers.
Then came the smell: not rotting kelp, but the sharp, medicinal coldness of mineral needles. His gums went numb; his throat felt parched, dry as lime.
He backed into the center of the lantern room, his shoulders pressing against the brass pedestal of the dead lens.
“Callow?” Julian whispered.
From the bottom of the spiral stairs, something began to ascend. Each step produced a slow, wet suction, followed by the faint tinkling chime of dry crystals breaking underfoot.
A voice answered from the dark curve of the staircase—flat, hollow, and muffled by a throat lined with stone:

“The hatch was unbolted, Vance. You forgot the salt.”

Julian lunged forward to throw the trapdoor shut, but his hand froze above the ring.
Drifting up through the open well of the stair came no shadow, no silhouette. Only a dense, pale fog of dry white needles, rising on the draft like a cloud of agitated moths, sparkling cold in the dark.
